title: The Torment of Individualism
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/heather-penatzer
text:
Across forty years, Tom Cruise’s career has chronicled the decline and fall of America in the public imagination. When Top Gun first appeared in 1986, its celebration of American military prowess and individual daring captured the nation’s self-conception near its acme, late in the Cold War. Cruise’s Pete “Maverick” Mitchell embodied a distinctly American ideal of heroism: the talented but insubordinate individual whose disregard for institutional authority is ultimately vindicated by his exceptional abilities. It is a character Cruise has spent much of his career reprising, most notably as the seemingly indestructible Ethan Hunt of the Mission: Impossible franchise, who routinely rescues the world from catastrophes its governments and institutions are powerless to prevent.

Cruise plays a very different role in Alejandro Iñárritu’s Digger, as the titular Digger Rockwell: a swashbuckling oil tycoon with a distinctly Texan drawl. Rather than the all-American hero, Digger embodies the excesses of American capitalism, his greed precipitating an environmental catastrophe that leaves much of Europe underwater. Here, it seems, is another Hollywood disaster movie, complete with familiar moralizing about corporate greed, environmental destruction, and American hubris.

Except Cruise isn’t Digger, and this isn’t a typical disaster movie. Forty minutes into the film, we discover that Cruise is actually Curtis Markson, an actor portraying Digger in a stage production called Fossil Fools, whose rehearsal we’ve been watching since the start of the movie. A celebrated work of political satire within the film’s universe, Fossil Fools falls somewhere between social commentary and overdone farce. This is the first in a remarkable sequence of revelations that repeatedly recontextualize the narrative, calling into question not only what the audience has seen but also what the right interpretation of it should be. And beneath its apparent cynicism, Digger is also a celebration of the American artistic tradition, whose greatest works have often leveled the most withering critiques of the nation.

Digger Rockwell is both savior and scapegoat in Markson’s portrayal. His story is rife with biblical motifs: his grandfather’s forty days and forty nights of digging before striking oil, the cross emblazoned on his Western belt buckle, and an imagined miracle involving loaves and fishes that he performs in exile. These messianic allusions culminate in a remarkable ten-minute monologue, delivered by Cruise with the fervor of a Southern preacher and captured by Iñárritu in a single continuous take. The centerpiece of an electric performance, Cruise’s manic energy and physicality transform what might otherwise be a pedestrian caricature of “Americanism” into a remarkably persuasive indictment of its critics, delivered by the very man meant to embody its worst excesses.

Appearing before an assembly of the European Community, who are searching for someone to blame for an unprecedented environmental disaster, Digger launches into an explosive denunciation of his accusers’ hypocrisy. He admits that his company’s drilling precipitated the catastrophe, yet he questions why the Europeans, who have profited from his operations and remain dependent on his product, should be absolved of responsibility for its consequences. Why hasn’t he been forced to stop drilling? “BECAUSE YOU DON’T WANT ME TO,” Digger bellows. The Eurocrats dissolve into a chaotic chorus of “blah blah blah,” their bureaucratic platitudes collapsing into theatrical absurdity.

A porous fourth wall focuses attention on specific moments. At one such point, Digger turns toward a cellphone camera to address “all you good folks at home watching this right now,” extending his accusations beyond the fictional audience. His defense is plainly self-serving, but it contains an uncomfortable truth: The world’s appetite for the products of his industry cannot be separated from the destruction that industry produces. “Freedom!” Digger cries, “That is what I supply. You demand, I supply.” The world condemning Digger has been only too happy to enjoy the fruits of his industry, provided someone else can be made to answer for the consequences. Nevertheless, the audience of Fossil Fools are content to make him the embodiment of their collective sins. The play culminates in his suicide, drawing frenzied applause as the magnate is sent to “meet his maker,” carrying with him the sins of the modern world. Whether his death has accomplished anything is another matter.

The film’s successive revelations complicate not only Digger’s culpability but also the authenticity of the story itself. What initially appears to be political satire is revealed as a theatrical production, seemingly lowering the stakes of its outrageous proceedings. Then we learn that Fossil Fools is based on real events, giving the viewer whiplash as the gravity of its story takes a new form. Finally, the revelation that Digger’s nephew, Kenny Rockwell, is the production’s principal financier calls the entire narrative into question. Kenny has purchased the rights to the story and influenced its presentation, even anonymizing his childhood self as “Kyle” in a signal that the facts were not faithfully represented in the story’s adaption.

This manipulation of history is at the center of Markson’s growing frustration with his director, Hannah, particularly over the production’s gratuitous attacks on Americans. Initially, Markson appears to be a self-serious actor insisting on giving a slapstick comedy the gravity of serious drama. Hannah complains that he is trying to turn the production into “fucking O’Neill,” ironically invoking one of America’s greatest playwrights in a tirade against American culture. Yet the revelation that Fossil Fools recounts actual events lends Markson’s objections a different significance. He takes a stand not just for his own freedom of artistic interpretation but in favor of the faithful representation of history itself, drawing a distinction between the American tradition of criticizing its own society and the simple contempt for Americans that passes for satire in Fossil Fools.

Hannah’s own independence is then undermined when Kenny dismissively explains that he hired her because she is “hip, or something.” Far from the independent artistic authority she initially appears to be, Hannah is another pawn of the powerful. The audience is not simply witnessing a story of manipulation; it is itself being manipulated by the story.

The film’s skepticism extends beyond those who control the narrative to those who imagine themselves morally exempt from the conduct it depicts. Riz Ahmed’s delightful performance as Dr. Nirav Ganesh, Rockwell United’s head of environmental safety and security, initially offers the audience an apparent moral surrogate. An Anthony Fauci-like straight man amid a cast of foolish fossils, Ganesh seems the only sane and principled figure in Digger’s orbit—the protagonist within the genre of film that Digger takes aim at. Yet Ganesh is no hero.

Having been “poached from EPA” to work for Big Oil, Ganesh has already compromised his principles, and despite his efforts, he unwittingly helps Digger turn events to his advantage. In one particularly memorable scene, Digger tricks Ganesh into eating toro, a fatty cut of tuna, against Ganesh’s insistence that he “tries not to” consume the fish. As Digger observes, “the only difference between trying not to eat tuna and not eating tuna is that sometimes you do.”

Ganesh is not simply a hypocrite but an illustration of the distance between moral intention and actual conduct. The same is true of Digger’s customers, the spectators of Fossil Fools, and ultimately the audience watching Digger itself. After a decade of treating “good” consumption as the performance of moral virtue, Digger asks whether the distinction between good and bad consumers was ever much of a distinction at all. 

Yet the film’s refusal to grant its characters moral innocence should not be mistaken for a rejection of the culture that produced them. Along with its explicit disdain for the tired tropes about American vulgarity, Digger displays an extraordinary affection for American artistic achievement and the country’s capacity for self-criticism. Hudson River School-inspired landscapes and Olin Herman Travis’s New Deal-era murals adorn the sets, juxtaposing romantic visions of the American landscape and industrial progress with the destruction wrought by modernity.

The film also situates itself within an American cinematic tradition preoccupied with the relationship between artifice, identity, and reality. The cries of “Silencio” preceding Digger’s monologue recall the Club Silencio sequence in David Lynch’s Mulholland Drive (2001), itself an exercise in exposing the illusions underlying theatrical performance. The prominent reference to John Cassavetes’ Opening Night (1977), similarly concerned with the boundaries between identity and performance, makes this inheritance more explicit. Perhaps the closest analogue is Citizen Kane, with its fictionalized and nonlinear biography of an American magnate, its pointed critiques of how the powerful control the public narrative, and its examination of the torment of individualism. These references are more than affectionate allusions. In its willingness to experiment with cinematic form, to expose the mechanisms through which stories acquire their authority, and to turn its criticism on the society that produced it, Digger participates in the very tradition it celebrates.

Cruise himself may be the film’s most important cultural reference. The exceptional American individual who once saved the world has become the exceptional individual whose demise provides a false salvation. Both fantasies locate responsibility for the fate of civilization in a single man, obscuring the collective forces that have brought it to the brink of catastrophe.

Much of the criticism of Digger, which is shaping up to be a box-office bomb, has focused on its supposed heavy-handedness, its tendency to announce rather than imply its convictions. Yet the variety of interpretations it has inspired suggests that, for all its apparent directness, the film has hardly succeeded in dictating what its audience will believe. There is a certain irony in this. A film so preoccupied with the manipulation of narratives cannot itself control the meanings audiences assign to it. For all its pessimism and insistence that art will not save us, the polarizing reception of Iñárritu’s masterpiece against the backdrop of our own world’s dangerous and unfettered technological advances offers a modest reassurance: Whatever else humanity may surrender to the forces it has unleashed, the creation and interpretation of art remain stubbornly human endeavors.
